claim: Diptericin A has a segregating amino acid polymorphism at the 69th residue of the mature 83-residue peptide in D. melanogaster and D. simulans.
source: In both D. melanogaster and Drosophila simulans, an amino acid polymorphism at the 69th residue of the mature 83-residue Diptericin peptide segregates in most populations surveyed (Unckless et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Unckless et al., 2016

claim: The amino acid polymorphism in Diptericin A is due to a point mutation that changes the ancestral serine (S) allele to arginine (R).
source: In both species, this polymorphism is due to a point mutation that changes the ancestral serine (S) allele to arginine (R), but the two species use different codons for arginine.
evidence: Supported by citation to Unckless et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence

claim: Homozygous serine flies have better survival rate 5 days post infection with P. rettgeri (~60%) than homozygous arginine flies (~20%) or flies with a premature stop codon in diptericin (0%).
source: The study used inbred fly lines and found homozygous serine flies have a better survival rate 5 days post infection (~60%) than homozygous arginine flies (~20%) or flies with a premature stop codon in diptericin (0%).
evidence: Supported by citation to Unckless et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing was used to create arginine allele (dptS69R), null alleles (Δdpt), and control serine allele (dptS69) in diptericin.
source: To control genetic background, we used CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing to create both an arginine allele (single nucleotide change, dptS69R) and multiple null alleles (1 or 3 base pair deletions, Δdpt flies), as well as control dptS69 (serine at position 69 of the mature peptide) in diptericin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Describes experimental methods performed in this study

claim: In systemic infection challenges with P. rettgeri, dptS69 flies are better protected from infection than dptS69R flies (p=5.42e-08) and Δdpt flies (p=6.46e-09).
source: In systemic infection challenges with P. rettgeri, dptS69 flies are better protected from infection than dptS69R flies (p=5.42e-08) and Δdpt flies (p=6.46e-09, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 1A

claim: For both inbred lines and CRISPR/Cas9-edited lines, survival for 5 days post infection with P. rettgeri is 50-60% for serine allele lines, 10-20% for arginine allele lines, and less than 5% for null alleles.
source: Remarkably, for inbred lines and CRISPR/Cas9-edited lines, survival for 5 days post infection with P. rettgeri for the serine allele lines is 50–60%, with the arginine allele is 10–20%, and less than 5% for null alleles.
evidence: Summarizes experimental data from both inbred and CRISPR lines

claim: DptS69 flies survived better than dptS69R flies for all systemic infections tested.
source: DptS69 flies survived better than dptS69R flies for all systemic infections tested (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1

claim: In Gram-positive bacterial infections (E. faecalis, S. succinus, L. fusiformis, and L. lactis), dptS69R flies had lower survival than Δdpt or imd- flies.
source: In the Gram-positive bacterial infections (E. faecalis, S. succinus, L. fusiformis, and L. lactis), dptS69R flies had lower survival than that of Δdpt or imd- (null allele for the Imd gene) flies (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E

claim: For S. marcescens systemic infection, dpt genotype did not affect survival except for imd- flies which die very quickly.
source: The only systemic infection where dpt genotype did not seem to matter was S. marcescens, where all flies survive infection well except for imd-, which die very quickly (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Females showed lower survival compared to males after systemic infection with E. faecalis (p=0.0003).
source: Females showed lower survival compared to males after systemic infection with E. faecalis (p=0.0003).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value

claim: Higher male survival post infection was observed previously for both E. faecalis and P. rettgeri, with differences ascribed to the Toll pathway.
source: Higher male survival post infection was observed previously for both E. faecalis and P. rettgeri, with differences ascribed to the Toll pathway (Duneau et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duneau et al., 2017

claim: Flies with functional copies of diptericin (dptS69 or dptS69R) did not differ in lifespan for either sex in axenic conditions (pgenotype=0.3762).
source: Flies with functional copies of diptericin (dptS69 or dptS69R) did not differ in lifespan for either sex (pgenotype=0.3762), and Δdpt lines show a similar lifespan.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value

claim: There was a difference in overall lifespan between the sexes among the CRISPR genome-edited lines in axenic conditions (psex=1.04e-6).
source: However, there was a difference in overall lifespan between the sexes among the CRISPR genome-edited lines (psex=1.04e-6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value

claim: In dptS69 or Δdpt lines, female flies have a longer lifespan than male flies in axenic conditions.
source: In dptS69 or Δdpt, female flies have a longer lifespan than male flies, as observed generally for D. melanogaster previously (Lints et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Lints et al., 2009

claim: Imd- male flies have a much longer lifespan than any of the other lines tested in axenic conditions.
source: In contrast, imd- male flies have a much longer lifespan than any of the other lines tested (Figure 2A – axenic row, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: After mono-association with L. plantarum, female Δdpt and female imd- flies both succumbed quickly post-feeding.
source: Flies that were fed L. plantarum show the most striking differences. Male flies continued to show similar lifespans to each other, but female Δdpt and female imd- flies both succumbed quickly post-feeding, indicating functional Diptericin is important for gut immunity against opportunistic L. plantarum in females.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference about the role of Diptericin

claim: Functional Diptericin is important for gut immunity against opportunistic L. plantarum in females.
source: Flies that were fed L. plantarum show the most striking differences. Male flies continued to show similar lifespans to each other, but female Δdpt and female imd- flies both succumbed quickly post-feeding, indicating functional Diptericin is important for gut immunity against opportunistic L. plantarum in females.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential survival of Δdpt and imd- females

claim: After mono-association with P. rettgeri, there is no significant difference in survival between dptS69 and dptS69R genotypes in either sex (p=0.612).
source: After mono-association, however, we see no significant difference between the two genotypes with P. rettgeri in either sex (p=0.612, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 2B

claim: Null Imd females die much earlier when fed P. rettgeri, while null Imd males survive much longer.
source: Surprisingly, however, the null allele for Imd again shows a significant effect on survival in a sex-specific manner: null Imd females die much earlier, and null Imd males survive much longer when fed P. rettgeri.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing sex-specific survival patterns

claim: Females eat more in a single hour of feeding than males.
source: We noted that females did eat more in a single hour of feeding, but that there was also an effect of diptericin genotype (with null flies eating less, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Diptericin genotype affects feeding rate, with null flies eating less.
source: We noted that females did eat more in a single hour of feeding, but that there was also an effect of diptericin genotype (with null flies eating less, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Female Δdpt and imd- flies had a much shorter lifespan than flies with functional Diptericin when poly-associated with L. plantarum and A. tropicalis.
source: We found that female Δdpt and imd- flies had a much shorter lifespan than flies with functional Diptericin (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: DptS69R female flies live longer than dptS69 female flies when poly-associated with L. plantarum and A. tropicalis (p=0.00782).
source: However, we observe that the diptericin genotype influences survival when poly-associated with L. plantarum and A. tropicalis. DptS69R female flies live longer than dptS69 female flies (Figure 2A and B; p=0.00782).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 2A and B

claim: The longer lifespan of dptS69R female flies compared to dptS69 female flies in poly-association with L. plantarum and A. tropicalis may indicate a trade-off between defense against systemic and gut immunity.
source: This is the opposite of systemic infections, where dptS69 flies always survived better than dptS69R flies, and may indicate a trade-off between defense against systemic and gut immunity.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of systemic infection and poly-association data

claim: In poly-association with L. plantarum and P. rettgeri, female Δdpt and imd- flies have a shorter lifespan than female dptS69 and dptS69R flies.
source: In poly-association with 1:1 L. plantarum and P. rettgeri, we observe many of the same patterns as in the poly-association with L. plantarum and A. tropicalis. Again, female Δdpt and imd- flies have a shorter lifespan than female dptS69 and dptS69R flies (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: DptS69R females have a longer lifespan than dptS69 flies when poly-associated with L. plantarum and P. rettgeri (p=0.000198).
source: DptS69R females have a longer lifespan than dptS69 flies (p=0.000198, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 2B

claim: There was no difference in survival between the sexes after systemic infection with L. plantarum in conventionally reared flies.
source: We saw no difference in survival between the sexes, as observed for systemic infections with E. faecalis or P. rettgeri, and saw no difference between Δdpt lines and lines with functional Diptericin, as observed for axenic flies mono-associated with L. plantarum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: DptS69 male flies survived better than dptS69R male flies after systemic infection with L. plantarum (p=0.00438).
source: Further, dptS69 male flies survived better than dptS69R male flies (p=0.00438), in line with observations from other systemic infections in males (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 1

claim: Bacterial load differences between genotypes in L. plantarum mono-association occur within the first 2 days post feeding but begin to disappear by day 20 (pgenotype(day2)=2.6e-5, pgenotype(day20)=0.709).
source: When specifically looking at mono-association with L. plantarum, we observe that bacterial load differences between genotypes occur within the first 2 days post feeding but begin to disappear by day 20 (pgenotype(day2)=2.6e-5, pgenotype(day20)=0.709, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance values and reference to Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: There is a genotype effect between dptS69 and dptS69R on P. rettgeri bacterial load on day 10 and 20 post feeding in males (pgenotype(day10)=0.0044, pgenotype(day20)=0.0004).
source: We also observed a genotype effect between dptS69 and dptS69R on day 10 and 20 post feeding in males (pgenotype(day10)=0.0044, pgenotype(day20)=0.0004, model only included dptS69 and dptS69R, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance values

claim: Bacterial load in dptS69R flies is higher than in dptS69 flies on day 10 and 20 post feeding with P. rettgeri in males.
source: In both instances, bacterial load in dptS69R flies is higher than in dptS69 flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the preceding sentence

claim: P. rettgeri establishes poorly in the gut of wildtype flies.
source: It is also important to note that P. rettgeri establishes poorly in the gut of wildtype flies (personal observation), which may explain the noisy results for mono-associations after oral infection.
evidence: Based on personal observation by the authors

claim: There were no statistically significant differences between dptS69 and dptS69R bacterial load for poly-association with L. plantarum and P. rettgeri.
source: There were no statistically significant differences between dptS69 and dptS69R bacterial for this poly-association (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 6

claim: L. plantarum shows differences in bacterial load on day 2 post feeding in poly-association with P. rettgeri (p=7.97e-6).
source: In fact, there were no significant differences between any of the P. rettgeri bacterial loads; however, L. plantarum does show differences on day 2 post feeding (p=7.97e-6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value

claim: Both Δdpt and imd- flies had higher L. plantarum bacterial load than dptS69 and dptS69R flies on day 2 post feeding in poly-association with P. rettgeri.
source: These differences are mainly between flies with nonfunctional diptericin (imd- and Δdpt) and flies with functional diptericin. Both Δdpt and imd- flies had higher bacterial load than dptS69 and dptS69R flies on day 2 post feeding, which may be an indication of the reason both these lines quickly succumb to feeding with L. plantarum, at least in the context of the poly-association with P. rettgeri.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference about the cause of mortality

claim: When subjecting male CRISPR/Cas9 flies to desiccation, conventionally reared flies succumb faster to desiccation stress than axenically reared flies (pgenotype<2e-16).
source: When subjecting our male CRISPR/Cas9 flies to desiccation, we observe conventionally reared flies succumb faster to desiccation stress than axenically reared flies (Figure 4A, pgenotype<2e-16).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 4A

claim: In conventionally reared males, dptS69 flies have similar desiccation resistance to dptS69R flies (p=0.917).
source: In conventionally reared males, dptS69 flies have similar desiccation resistance to dptS69R flies (p=0.917).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value

claim: DptS69 flies survive desiccation stress better than dptS69R flies when reared axenically (pgenotype=0.04126).
source: However, dptS69 flies survive desiccation stress better than dptS69R flies when reared axenically (pgenotype=0.04126).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value

claim: Axenically reared flies survive starvation stress better than conventionally reared flies (ptreatment<2e-16).
source: As with desiccation resistance, we found axenically reared flies survive starvation stress better than conventionally reared flies (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, ptreatment<2e-16).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Both conventionally reared and axenically reared dptS69R flies survive starvation stress longer than dptS69 flies (conventional: pgenotype<2e-16, axenic: pgenotype<2e-16).
source: However, unlike the desiccation stress conditions, both conventionally reared and axenically reared dptS69R flies survive starvation stress longer than dptS69 flies (conventional: pgenotype<2e-16, axenic: pgenotype<2e-16).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance values

claim: In conventionally reared flies, there is no difference in starvation survival between dptS69 flies and Δdpt flies.
source: In conventionally reared flies, there is no difference in survival between dptS69 flies and Δdpt flies (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 8

claim: In axenically reared flies, Δdpt flies have an intermediate starvation survival phenotype between dptS69 and dptS69R flies.
source: However, in axenically reared flies, Δdpt flies have an intermediate survival phenotype between dptS69 and dptS69R flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Female flies have a longer lifespan than males in conventionally reared flies (psex=5.80e-13) regardless of dpt genotype.
source: Female flies have a longer lifespan than males (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, psex=5.80e-13) regardless of dpt genotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: In conventionally reared males, dptS69 flies had a significantly longer lifespan than male dptS69R flies (mean of 60.3 days for dptS69 and 54.1 days for dptS69R, p=0.0072).
source: In males, dptS69 flies had a significantly longer lifespan than male dptS69R flies (mean of 60.3 days for dptS69 and 54.1 days for dptS69R, p=0.0072), but not in female flies (mean of 61.9 days for dptS69 and 59.0 days for dptS69R, p=0.6434).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with mean values and statistical significance values

claim: In conventionally reared females, there is no significant difference in lifespan between dptS69 and dptS69R flies (mean of 61.9 days for dptS69 and 59.0 days for dptS69R, p=0.6434).
source: In males, dptS69 flies had a significantly longer lifespan than male dptS69R flies (mean of 60.3 days for dptS69 and 54.1 days for dptS69R, p=0.0072), but not in female flies (mean of 61.9 days for dptS69 and 59.0 days for dptS69R, p=0.6434).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with mean values and statistical significance values

claim: In conventionally reared flies, female flies with the longest lifespan have nonfunctional Diptericin (Δdpt line and imd- line).
source: Interestingly, the female flies with the longest lifespan have nonfunctional Diptericin (Figure 4C, Δdpt line and imd- line, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 9

claim: Males lacking functional Diptericin show increased lifespan, but to a lesser extent than females.
source: Males lacking functional Diptericin show the same effect, but to a lesser extent.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the context

claim: In the presence of a standard gut microbiota, both Dpt and a functional Imd pathway may decrease longevity.
source: These results provide evidence that, in the presence of a standard gut microbiota, both Dpt and a functional Imd pathway may decrease longevity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing increased longevity in Δdpt and imd- flies

claim: Downregulation of NF-κB pathways and AMPs increased lifespan in Drosophila.
source: This is consistent with others who found downregulation of NF-κB pathways and AMPs increased lifespan in Drosophila (Lin et al., 2018; Khor and Cai, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2018 and Khor and Cai, 2020

claim: Flies that were co-reared in cages had similar microbiomes, with no discernible differences by Shannon diversity (p=0.5239).
source: First, we found flies that were co-reared in cages had similar microbiomes, with no discernible differences by the alpha diversity metric, Shannon diversity (p=0.5239, Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 5A

claim: The microbiomes of flies reared in vials were distinctly different overall compared to the microbiomes of flies reared in the cages (p<0.001).
source: On the other hand, the microbiomes of flies reared in vials were distinctly different overall compared to the microbiomes of flies reared in the cages (p<0.001, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance value and reference to Figure 5B

claim: There was a significant difference between the 2 dptS69R lines used in vial-reared flies.
source: There were 2 dptS69R lines used, and even though these are the same genotype and genetic background, there was a significant difference between the 2 lines (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The difference between the 2 dptS69R lines is likely due to within-vial drift in gut microbiome communities.
source: This difference is likely due to the within-vial drift in gut microbiome communities (Wong et al., 2013), which we attempted to control for using flies of different genotypes reared in the same cage (Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from experimental design and supported by citation to Wong et al., 2013

claim: Dpt genotype does not affect the overall composition of the microbiome of wild-caught flies based on Shannon diversity and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity.
source: We found that dpt genotype does not affect the overall composition of the microbiome of wild-caught flies based on Shannon diversity (alpha diversity) and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (beta diversity) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous serine flies have a slightly higher abundance of Morganellaceae family reads than homozygous arginine flies, but these differences were not significant.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous serine flies have a slightly higher abundance than homozygous arginine flies (Figure 5D), but these differences were not significant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: P. rettgeri belongs to the Morganellaceae family.
source: Most intriguing is the difference in abundance of Morganellaceae family reads since P. rettgeri belongs to this family.
evidence: Based on established taxonomic knowledge

claim: The innate immune system provides hosts with a crucial first line of defense against pathogens.
source: The innate immune system provides hosts with a crucial first line of defense against pathogens.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Immune genes are often among the fastest evolving genes in the genome.
source: While immune genes are often among the fastest evolving genes in the genome, in Drosophila, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are notable exceptions.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: In Drosophila, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are notable exceptions to the pattern of rapid evolution of immune genes.
source: While immune genes are often among the fastest evolving genes in the genome, in Drosophila, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are notable exceptions.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript

claim: AMPs may be under balancing selection, such that over evolutionary timescales, multiple alleles are maintained in populations.
source: Instead, AMPs may be under balancing selection, such that over evolutionary timescales, multiple alleles are maintained in populations.
evidence: Based on inference from population genetic patterns

claim: Diptericin A helps control opportunistic gut infections by common Drosophila gut microbes, especially those of Lactobacillus plantarum.
source: Diptericin A also helps control opportunistic gut infections by common Drosophila gut microbes, especially those of Lactobacillus plantarum.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: There are strong sex-specific effects on gut immunity that are most prominent in flies without functional diptericin A.
source: In addition to genotypic effects on gut immunity, we also see strong sex-specific effects that are most prominent in flies without functional diptericin A.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Flies that are homozygous for one allele of diptericin A are better equipped to survive a systemic infection from P. rettgeri.
source: Overall, we find flies that are homozygous for one allele of diptericin A are better equipped to survive a systemic infection from P. rettgeri, but in general have a shorter lifespans after being fed common gut commensals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Flies homozygous for the serine allele of diptericin A in general have shorter lifespans after being fed common gut commensals.
source: Overall, we find flies that are homozygous for one allele of diptericin A are better equipped to survive a systemic infection from P. rettgeri, but in general have a shorter lifespans after being fed common gut commensals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A possible mechanism for the maintenance of genetic variation of diptericin A is through the complex interactions of sex, systemic immunity, and the maintenance of the gut microbiome.
source: Our results suggest a possible mechanism for the maintenance of genetic variation of diptericin A through the complex interactions of sex, systemic immunity, and the maintenance of the gut microbiome.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results presented in the manuscript

claim: An excessive immune response causes damage to self either directly (autoimmunity, cytokine storms) or through dysbiosis via disruption of the composition of beneficial microflora.
source: However, an excessive immune response causes damage to self either directly (autoimmunity, cytokine storms) or through dysbiosis via disruption of the composition of beneficial microflora (Miyauchi et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2020; Badinloo et al., 2018; Fajgenbaum and June, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miyauchi et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2020; Badinloo et al., 2018; Fajgenbaum and June, 2020

claim: The immune system must distinguish harmful vs. beneficial microbes in each context.
source: The challenge of maintaining a balanced immune response is exacerbated because the threat of microorganisms is contextual; thus, the immune system must distinguish harmful vs. beneficial microbes in each context (Thaiss et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thaiss et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017

claim: An ingested microbe may be harmless or even beneficial as a food source in the digestive tract, but when in circulation, that same microbe may prove harmful to the organism.
source: For example, an ingested microbe may be harmless or even beneficial as a food source in the digestive tract, but, when in circulation, that same microbe may prove harmful to the organism (Brown et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2012

claim: Balancing a robust innate immune system may lead to the maintenance of genetic polymorphism in genes that encode for proteins intimately involved in the immune response.
source: One consequence of balancing a robust innate immune system is that it may lead to the maintenance of genetic polymorphism in genes that encode for proteins intimately involved in the immune response (Bagnicka et al., 2010; Pierce et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bagnicka et al., 2010; Pierce et al., 2021

claim: Natural variation in many immune genes is maintained by balancing selection.
source: In contrast to the evolutionary arms race model, natural variation in many immune genes is maintained by balancing selection (Chapman et al., 2019; Aguilar et al., 2004; Ferrer-Admetlla et al., 2008; Tennessen and Blouin, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2019; Aguilar et al., 2004; Ferrer-Admetlla et al., 2008; Tennessen and Blouin, 2008

claim: The inference of balancing selection from molecular population genetic data is difficult, especially when genes are small and in areas of high recombination.
source: The inference of balancing selection from molecular population genetic data is difficult, especially when genes are small and in areas of high recombination.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in population genetics

claim: Several examples of balancing selection exist, many of which involve small effector proteins of the innate immune system.
source: Nonetheless, several examples of balancing selection exist, many of which involve small effector proteins of the innate immune system (Tennessen and Blouin, 2008; Unckless et al., 2016; Chapman et al., 2016; Padhi and Verghese, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tennessen and Blouin, 2008; Unckless et al., 2016; Chapman et al., 2016; Padhi and Verghese, 2008

claim: Invertebrates lack an adaptive immune system.
source: Invertebrates lack an adaptive immune system, so the delicate balance between systemic and gut immunity is achieved only through adjustments to the innate immune response (Ryu et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citation to Ryu et al., 2010

claim: The IMD pathway is the main NF-κB immune pathway in the gut and contributes to the maintenance of the microbiome and protection from gut infections.
source: Though first characterized for its role in systemic immunity, the (IMD) pathway is also the main NF-κB immune pathway in the gut and contributes to the maintenance of the microbiome and protection from gut infections (Lhocine et al., 2008; Bosco-Drayon et al., 2012; Broderick et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lhocine et al., 2008; Bosco-Drayon et al., 2012; Broderick et al., 2014

claim: The standard gut microbiome of lab-reared Drosophila melanogaster consists of two prominent bacterial genera: Lactobacillus and Acetobacter.
source: The standard gut microbiome of lab-reared Drosophila melanogaster consists of two prominent bacterial genera: Lactobacillus and Acetobacter (Broderick et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broderick et al., 2014

claim: AMPs are a critical part of the innate immune system that act as broad-spectrum antimicrobials, combating bacteria, fungi, and viruses.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a critical part of the innate immune system that act as broad-spectrum antimicrobials, combating bacteria, fungi, and viruses.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Dysregulation of AMPs has been connected to diseases such as atopic dermatitis and Alzheimer's disease.
source: AMPs have also been demonstrated to have critical roles in other physiological functions, e.g., dysregulation of AMPs has been connected to diseases such as atopic dermatitis and Alzheimer's disease (Wang et al., 2020; Ong et al., 2002; Rieg et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020; Ong et al., 2002; Rieg et al., 2005

claim: AMPs contribute to the aging process, where the immune system becomes more active as organisms age to compensate for a decline in its effectiveness, leading to cytotoxicity that shortens lifespan.
source: AMPs also contribute to the aging process, where the immune system becomes more active as organisms age to compensate for a decline in its effectiveness. However, this leads to cytotoxicity that in turn shortens lifespan (Badinloo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Badinloo et al., 2018

claim: In Drosophila, AMPs play a crucial role in both managing systemic infections and in the maintenance of the gut microbiota.
source: In Drosophila, AMPs play a crucial role in both managing systemic infections and in the maintenance of the gut microbiota (Buchon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buchon et al., 2014

claim: Drosophila AMPs appear to evolve more slowly than most immune gene families.
source: AMPs, however, appear to evolve more slowly than most immune gene families (Clark et al., 2007; Jiggins and Kim, 2007; Sackton et al., 2007; Obbard et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2007; Jiggins and Kim, 2007; Sackton et al., 2007; Obbard et al., 2009

claim: One explanation for the perceived lack of adaptive evolution in Drosophila AMPs is that their genetic variation is maintained adaptively through balancing selection.
source: One explanation for this perceived lack of adaptive evolution is that Drosophila AMPs' genetic variation is maintained adaptively through balancing selection (Chapman et al., 2019; Comeron, 2014; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016; Perlmutter et al., 2024), where different selective pressures favor different alleles.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2019; Comeron, 2014; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016; Perlmutter et al., 2024

claim: Naturally occurring allelic variation in AMP loci is sometimes associated with variability in pathogen resistance.
source: Naturally occurring allelic variation in AMP loci is sometimes associated with variability in pathogen resistance (Unckless et al., 2016; Lazzaro et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2023; Hanson et al., 2023a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Unckless et al., 2016; Lazzaro et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2023; Hanson et al., 2023a

claim: Diptericin A is one of the canonical effector genes of the Drosophila immune deficiency (IMD) pathway and is generally associated with defense against Gram-negative bacterial infection.
source: Diptericin A (hereon referred to as diptericin or Dpt) is one of the canonical effector genes of the Drosophila immune deficiency (IMD) pathway and is generally associated with defense against Gram-negative bacterial infection (Tanji et al., 2007; Broderick, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanji et al., 2007; Broderick, 2016

claim: At least six null alleles of dpt segregate in natural populations of D. melanogaster.
source: Note that while our study focuses on the serine/arginine polymorphism, at least six null alleles of dpt segregate in natural populations of D. melanogaster, and the frequency of those nulls shows clinal variation in both North America and Africa (Hanson et al., 2019b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanson et al., 2019b

claim: The frequency of null alleles of dpt shows clinal variation in both North America and Africa.
source: Note that while our study focuses on the serine/arginine polymorphism, at least six null alleles of dpt segregate in natural populations of D. melanogaster, and the frequency of those nulls shows clinal variation in both North America and Africa (Hanson et al., 2019b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanson et al., 2019b

claim: The null alleles of dpt are likely maintained selectively.
source: Note that while our study focuses on the serine/arginine polymorphism, at least six null alleles of dpt segregate in natural populations of D. melanogaster, and the frequency of those nulls shows clinal variation in both North America and Africa (Hanson et al., 2019b); thus, the nulls are likely maintained selectively too.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of clinal variation in null allele frequencies

claim: Evidence of clinal patterns in allele frequency exists in Africa and (to a lesser extent) North America.
source: This scenario is partly supported by the evidence of clinal patterns in allele frequency in Africa and (to a lesser extent) North America (Hanson et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanson et al., 2019a

claim: AMP overexpression and microbial proliferation are commonly observed in aging flies.
source: We then used axenic and gnotobiotic flies to look at the lifespan of flies since AMP overexpression and microbial proliferation are commonly observed in aging flies (Arias-Rojas and Iatsenko, 2022; Badinloo et al., 2018; Shit et al., 2022; Hanson and Lemaitre, 2023b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arias-Rojas and Iatsenko, 2022; Badinloo et al., 2018; Shit et al., 2022; Hanson and Lemaitre, 2023b
